exampleAnswers.title: Solving Equations Using the Power and Product Rules

question.explanation:
Notice that the logarithms share the same base.

First, we apply the power rule to the second term to make the coefficient in front of each logarithm the same:

\begin{align*} \log_{3} (72x) + 2\log_{3} x &= 2 \\[5pt] \log_{3} (72x) + \log_{3} (x^2) &= 2 \end{align*}

Next, we combine the logarithms using the product rule. This gives

\begin{align*} \log_{3} (72x \cdot x^2) &= 2\\[5pt] \log_{3} (72x^3) &= 2. \end{align*}

Writing this equation in its equivalent exponential form, we get

\begin{align*} 3^{\log_{3} (72x^3)} &= 3^{2}\\[5pt] 72x^3&= 9 \end{align*}

Now, we solve this quadratic equation for $x$ using the usual methods.

\begin{align*} x^3 &= \dfrac{1}{8} \\[5pt] x &= \sqrt[3]{\dfrac{1}{8}} \\[5pt] x &= \dfrac{1}{2} \end{align*}

Let's now check for extraneous solutions by substituting back into the original equation:

  • Substituting $x=\dfrac{1}{2}$ back into the original equation, we get \begin{align*} \log_{3} \left(72\cdot \dfrac{1}{2}\right) + 2\log_{3} \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right) &\stackrel{?}{=} 2\\[5pt] \log_{3} 36+ \log_{3} \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^2 &\stackrel{?}{=} 2\\[5pt] \log_{3} 36 + \log_{3} \left(\dfrac{1}{4}\right) &\stackrel{?}{=} 2\\[5pt] \log_{3} \left(36\cdot \dfrac{1}{4}\right) &\stackrel{?}{=} 2\\[5pt] \log_{3} (9) &\stackrel{?}{=} 2\\[5pt] 2&=2.\quad{\color{green}{\checkmark}} \end{align*} Therefore, $x=\dfrac{1}{2}$ is a valid solution.

Therefore, the correct answer is "$x=\dfrac{1}{2}$ only."

example.title: Solving Equations Using the Power and Product Rules

question.explanation:
Notice that the logarithms share the same base.

First, we apply the power rule to the second term to make the coefficient in front of each logarithm the same:

\begin{align*} \log_{5} \left(\dfrac{x^2}{2}\right) + \dfrac13\log_{5} (8x^3) &= 3 \\[5pt] \log_{5} \left(\dfrac{x^2}{2}\right) + \log_{5} \left((8x^3)^{1/3}\right) &= 3 \\[5pt] \log_{5} \left(\dfrac{x^2}{2}\right) + \log_{5} \left(2x\right) &= 3 \end{align*}

Next, we combine the logarithms using the product rule. This gives

\begin{align*} \log_{5} \left(\dfrac{x^2}{2} \cdot 2x\right) &= 3\\[5pt] \log_{5} (x^3) &= 3. \end{align*}

Writing this equation in its equivalent exponential form, we get

\begin{align*} 5^{\log_{5} (x^3)} &= 5^{3}\\[5pt] x^3&= 125 \end{align*}

Now, we solve this equation for $x$ using the usual methods.

\begin{align*} x^3 &= 125 \\[5pt] x &= \sqrt[3]{125} \\[5pt] x &= 5 \end{align*}

Let's now check for extraneous solutions by substituting back into the original equation:

  • Substituting $x=5$ back into the original equation, we get \begin{align*} \log_{5} \left(\dfrac{5^2}{2}\right) + \dfrac13\log_{5} (8\cdot 5^3) &\stackrel{?}{=} 3\\[5pt] \log_{5} \left(\dfrac{25}{2}\right) +\log_{5} \left((8\cdot 5^3)^{1/3}\right) &\stackrel{?}{=} 3\\[5pt] \log_{5} \left(\dfrac{25}{2}\right) +\log_{5} \left((2^3\cdot 5^3)^{1/3}\right) &\stackrel{?}{=} 3\\[5pt] \log_{5} \left(\dfrac{25}{2}\right) +\log_{5} (10) &\stackrel{?}{=} 3\\[5pt] \log_{5} \left( \dfrac{25}{2} \cdot 10\right) &\stackrel{?}{=} 3\\[5pt] \log_{5} \left( 125\right) &\stackrel{?}{=} 3\\[5pt] 3&=3.\quad{\color{green}{\checkmark}} \end{align*} Therefore, $x=5$ is a valid solution.

Therefore, the correct answer is "$x=5$ only."

example.title: Solving Equations Using the Power and Product Rules

question.explanation:
Notice that the logarithms share the same base.

First, we apply the power rule to the first term to make the coefficient in front of each logarithm the same:

\begin{align*} 2\log_{18} (3x) + \log_{18} x &= 1 \\[5pt] \log_{18} \left((3x)^2\right) + \log_{18} x &= 1 \\[5pt] \log_{18} (9x^2) + \log_{18} x &= 1 \end{align*}

Next, we combine the logarithms using the product rule. This gives

\begin{align*} \log_{18} (9x^2 \cdot x) &= 1 \\[5pt] \log_{18} (9x^3) &= 1. \end{align*}

Writing this equation in its equivalent exponential form, we get

\begin{align*} 18^{\log_{18} (9x^3)} &= 18^{1}\\[5pt] 9x^3 &= 18 \end{align*}

Now, we solve this quadratic equation for $x$ using the usual methods.

\begin{align*} x^3 &= 2 \\[5pt] x &= \sqrt[3]{2} \end{align*}

Let's now check for an extraneous solution by substituting back into the original equation:

  • Substituting $x=\sqrt[3]{2}$ back into the original equation, we get \begin{align*} 2\log_{18} (3\cdot \sqrt[3]{2}) + \log_{18} \sqrt[3]{2} &\stackrel{?}{=} 1\\[5pt] \log_{18} \left((3\sqrt[3]{2})^2\right) + \log_{18} \sqrt[3]{2} &\stackrel{?}{=} 1\\[5pt] \log_{18} \left((3^2\sqrt[3]{2^2}\right) + \log_{18} \sqrt[3]{2} &\stackrel{?}{=} 1\\[5pt] \log_{18} 9\sqrt[3]{4} + \log_{18} \sqrt[3]{2} &\stackrel{?}{=} 1\\[5pt] \log_{18} (9\sqrt[3]{4}\cdot \sqrt[3]{2}) &\stackrel{?}{=} 1\\[5pt] \log_{18} \left(9\cdot\sqrt[3]{8}\right) &\stackrel{?}{=} 1\\[5pt] \log_{18} \left(9\cdot 2\right) &\stackrel{?}{=} 1\\[5pt] \log_{18} (18) &\stackrel{?}{=} 1\\[5pt] 1&=1.\quad{\color{green}{\checkmark}} \end{align*} Therefore, $x=\sqrt[3]{2}$ is a valid solution.

Therefore, the correct answer is "$x=\sqrt[3]{2}$ only."

example.title: Solving Equations Using the Power and Product Rules

question.explanation:
Notice that the logarithms share the same base.

First, we apply the power rule to the second term to make the coefficient in front of each logarithm the same:

\begin{align*} \log_8 2 + 2\log_8 (2x) &= 1 \\[5pt] \log_8 2 + \log_8 ((2x)^2) &= 1 \\[5pt] \log_8 2 + \log_8 (4x^2) &= 1 \end{align*}

Next, we combine the logarithms using the product rule. This gives

\begin{align*} \log_8 (2 \cdot 4x^2) &= 1 \\[5pt] \log_8 (8x^2) &= 1. \end{align*}

Writing this equation in its equivalent exponential form, we get

\begin{align*} 8^{\log_8 (8x^2)} &= 8^{1}\\[5pt] 8x^2 &= 8 \end{align*}

Now, we solve this quadratic equation for $x$ using the usual methods.

\begin{align*} x^2 &= 1 \\[5pt] x &= \pm 1 \end{align*}

Let's now check for extraneous solutions by substituting back into the original equation:

  • Substituting $x=1$ back into the original equation, we get \begin{align*} \log_8 2 + 2\log_8 (2\cdot 1) &\stackrel{?}{=} 1\\[5pt] \log_8 2 + 2\log_8 (2) &\stackrel{?}{=} 1\\[5pt] \log_8 2 + \log_8 (2^2) &\stackrel{?}{=} 1\\[5pt] \log_8 2 + \log_8 (4) &\stackrel{?}{=} 1\\[5pt] \log_8 (2\cdot 4) &\stackrel{?}{=} 1\\[5pt] \log_8 (8) &\stackrel{?}{=} 1\\[5pt] 1&=1.\quad{\color{green}{\checkmark}} \end{align*} Therefore, $x=1$ is a valid solution.

  • Substituting $x=-1$ back into the original equation, we get \begin{align*} \log_8 2 + 2\log_8 (2\cdot -1) &\stackrel{?}{=} 1 \\[5pt] \log_8 2 + 2\log_8 (-2) &\neq 1\quad{\color{red}{\times}} \end{align*} because $\log_8 (-2)$ is undefined. Therefore, $x=-1$ is not a valid solution.

Therefore, the correct answer is "$x=1$ only."

exampleAnswers.title: Solving Equations Using the Power and Quotient Rules

question.explanation:
Notice that the logarithms share the same base.

First, we apply the power rule to the first term to make the coefficient in front of each logarithm the same:

\begin{align*} \dfrac{1}{2}\log_2 64 - \log_2 \left(x^2\right) &= 1 \\[5pt] \log_2 (64)^{1/2} - \log_2 \left(x^2\right) &= 1 \\[5pt] \log_2 8 - \log_2 \left(x^2\right) &= 1 \end{align*}

Next, we combine the logarithms using the quotient rule. This gives

\begin{align*} \log_2 \left(\dfrac{8}{x^2}\right) &= 1. \end{align*}

Writing this equation in its equivalent exponential form, we get

\begin{align*} \dfrac{8}{x^2} &= 2^{1}\\[5pt] \dfrac{8}{x^2} &= 2 \end{align*}

Now, we solve this rational equation for $x$ using the usual methods.

\begin{align*} \require{cancel} x^2\cdot \dfrac{8}{x^2} &= x^2\cdot 2\\[5pt] \cancel{x^2}\cdot \dfrac{8}{\cancel{x^2}} &= 2x^2\\[5pt] 8 &=2x^2\\[5pt] \dfrac{8}{2} &=x^2\\[5pt] x^2 &=4 \\[5pt] x &=\pm 2 \end{align*}

Let's now check for extraneous solutions by substituting back into the original equation:

  • Substituting $x=2$ back into the original equation, we get \begin{align*} \dfrac{1}{2}\log_2 64 - \log_2 \left(2^2\right) &\stackrel{?}{=} 1 \\[5pt] \log_2\left(64^{1/2}\right) - \log_2 \left(4\right) &\stackrel{?}{=} 1 \\[5pt] \log_2(8) - \log_2 \left(4\right) &\stackrel{?}{=} 1 \\[5pt] 3-2 &\stackrel{?}{=} 1 \\[5pt] 1 &=1\quad{\color{green}{\checkmark}} \end{align*} Therefore, $x=2$ is a valid solution.

  • Substituting $x=-2$ back into the original equation, we get \begin{align*} \dfrac{1}{2}\log_2 64 - \log_2 \left((-2)^2\right) &\stackrel{?}{=} 1 \\[5pt] \log_2\left(64^{1/2}\right) - \log_2 \left(4\right) &\stackrel{?}{=} 1 \\[5pt] \log_2(8) - \log_2 \left(4\right) &\stackrel{?}{=} 1 \\[5pt] 3-2&\stackrel{?}{=} 1 \\[5pt] 1 &=1\quad{\color{green}{\checkmark}} \end{align*} Therefore, $x=-2$ is a valid solution.

Therefore, the correct answer is "$x=\pm 2.$"

example.title: Solving Equations Using the Power and Quotient Rules

question.explanation:
Notice that the logarithms share the same base.

First, we apply the power rule to the first term to make the coefficient in front of each logarithm the same:

\begin{align*} \dfrac{1}{2}\log_8 (16x^4) - \log_8 \left(\dfrac{1}{2x}\right) &= 1 \\[5pt] \log_8 \left(\left(16x^4\right)^{1/2}\right) - \log_8 \left(\dfrac{1}{2x}\right) &= 1 \\[5pt] \log_8 (4x^2) - \log_8\left(\dfrac{1}{2x} \right)&= 1 \end{align*}

Next, we combine the logarithms using the quotient rule. This gives

\begin{align*} \log_8 \left(\dfrac{4x^2}{\left(\dfrac{1}{2x} \right)}\right) &= 1\\[5pt] \log_8 \left(8x^3\right) & = 1. \end{align*}

Writing this equation in its equivalent exponential form, we get

\begin{align*} 8x^3 &= 8^1\\[5pt] 8x^3 &= 8 \end{align*}

Now, we solve this rational equation for $x$ using the usual methods.

\begin{align*} \require{cancel} \dfrac{8x^3}{8} &= \dfrac{8}{8}\\[5pt] \dfrac{\cancel{8}x^3}{\cancel{8}}&= 1\\[5pt] x^3 &=1\\[5pt] x &=1 \end{align*}

Let's now check for an extraneous solution by substituting back into the original equation:

  • Substituting $x=1$ back into the original equation, we get \begin{align*} \dfrac{1}{2}\log_8 (16\cdot 1^4) - \log_8 \left(\dfrac{1}{2\cdot 1}\right) &\stackrel{?}{=} 1 \\[5pt] \dfrac{1}{2}\log_8 16 - \log_8 \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right) &\stackrel{?}{=} 1 \\[5pt] \log_8 16^{1/2} - \log_8 \left( \dfrac{1}{2}\right) &\stackrel{?}{=} 1 \\[5pt] \log_8 4 - \log_8 \left(\dfrac{1}{2} \right) &\stackrel{?}{=} 1 \\[5pt] \log_8 \left(\dfrac{4}{\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)}\right) &\stackrel{?}{=} 1 \\[5pt] \log_8 \left(8\right) &\stackrel{?}{=} 1 \\[5pt] 1 &=1\quad{\color{green}{\checkmark}} \end{align*} Therefore, $x=1$ is a valid solution.

Therefore, the correct answer is "$x=1$ only."

exampleAnswers.title: Solving Equations Resulting in Rational Equations Using the Quotient Rule

question.explanation:
Notice that the logarithms share the same base.

First, we apply the power rule to the first term to make the coefficient in front of each logarithm the same:

\begin{align*} 2\log_5 (2x) - \log_5(x^2+1)&= \log_5 3 \\[5pt] \log_5 (4x^2) - \log_5(x^2+1) &= \log_5 3 \end{align*}

Next, we combine the logarithms on the left-hand side using the quotient rule:

\begin{align*} \log_5 \left(\dfrac {4x^2} {x^2+1} \right) &= \log_5 3 \end{align*}

Now, we solve the equation for $x$ using the usual methods.

\begin{align*} \require{cancel} \dfrac {4x^2} {x^2+1} &= 3 \\[5pt] (x^2+1)\cdot \dfrac {4x^2} {x^2+1} &= (x^2+1)\cdot 3 \\[5pt] \cancel{(x^2+1)}\cdot \dfrac {4x^2} {\cancel{x^2+1}} &= (x^2+1)\cdot 3 \\[5pt] 4x^2 &= 3x^2+ 3\\[5pt] x^2 & =3 \end{align*}

So, $x = -\sqrt 3$ or $x = \sqrt 3.$

Let's now check for extraneous solutions by substituting back into the original equation:

  • Substituting $x=-\sqrt 3$ back into the original equation, we get \begin{align*} 2\log_5 (2\cdot (-\sqrt 3)) - \log_5((-\sqrt 3)^2+1) &\stackrel{?}{=} \log_5 3\\[5pt] 2\log_5 (-2\sqrt 3) - \log_5(4) &\neq \log_5 3\quad{\color{red}{\times}} \end{align*} because $\log_5 (-2\sqrt 3)$ is undefined. Therefore, $x=-\sqrt3$ is not a valid solution.
  • Substituting $x=\sqrt 3$ back into the original equation, we get \begin{align*} 2\log_5 (2\cdot \sqrt 3) - \log_5((\sqrt 3)^2+1) &\stackrel{?}{=} \log_5 3\\[5pt] 2\log_5 (2\sqrt 3) - \log_5(4) &\stackrel{?}{=} \log_5 3\\[5pt] \log_5 \left((2\sqrt 3)^2\right) - \log_5(4) &\stackrel{?}{=} \log_5 3\\[5pt] \log_5 \left(12\right) - \log_5(4) &\stackrel{?}{=} \log_5 3\\[5pt] \log_5 \left(\dfrac{12}{4}\right) &= \log_5 3\quad{\color{green}{\checkmark}} \end{align*} Therefore, $x=\sqrt 3$ is a valid solution.

Therefore, the correct answer is "$x=\sqrt 3$ only".

example.title: Solving Equations Resulting in Rational Equations Using the Quotient Rule

question.explanation:
Notice that the logarithms share the same base.

First, we apply the power rule to the first term to make the coefficient in front of each logarithm the same:

\begin{align*} 2\log_6 (3x) - \log_6(2x^2+1)&= \log_6 3 \\[5pt] \log_6 (9x^2) - \log_6(2x^2+1) &= \log_6 3 \end{align*}

Next, we combine the logarithms on the left-hand side using the quotient rule:

\begin{align*} \log_6 \left(\dfrac {9x^2} {2x^2+1} \right) &= \log_6 3 \end{align*}

Now, we solve the equation for $x$ using the usual methods.

\begin{align*} \require{cancel} \dfrac {9x^2} {2x^2+1} &= 3 \\[5pt] (2x^2+1)\cdot \dfrac {9x^2} {2x^2+1} &= (2x^2+1)\cdot 3 \\[5pt] \cancel{(2x^2+1)}\cdot \dfrac {9x^2} {\cancel{2x^2+1}} &= (2x^2+1)\cdot 3 \\[5pt] 9x^2 &= 6x^2+ 3\\[5pt] 3x^2 & =3 \\[5pt] x^2 &= 1 \end{align*}

So, $x = -1$ or $x = 1.$

Let's now check for extraneous solutions by substituting back into the original equation:

  • Substituting $x=-1$ back into the original equation, we get \begin{align*} 2\log_6 (3\cdot (-1)) - \log_6(2(-1)^2+1) &\stackrel{?}{=} \log_6 3\\[5pt] 2\log_6 (-3) - \log_6(3) &\neq \log_6 3\quad{\color{red}{\times}} \end{align*} because $\log_6 (-3)$ is undefined. Therefore, $x=-1$ is not a valid solution.
  • Substituting $x=1$ back into the original equation, we get \begin{align*} 2\log_6 (3\cdot 1) - \log_6(2(1)^2+1) &\stackrel{?}{=} \log_6 3\\[5pt] 2\log_6 3 - \log_6 3 & \stackrel{?}{=} \log_6 3\\[5pt] (2-1) \log_6 3 & \stackrel{?}{=} \log_6 3\\[5pt] \log_6 3 &= \log_6 3\quad{\color{green}{\checkmark}} \end{align*} Therefore, $x=1$ is a valid solution.

Therefore, the correct answer is "$x=1$ only".
